Whitewater. An investigation that started with a failed real estate deal and spiraled into a four-year witch hunt that cost seventy million dollars and found nothing.

In 1978, Bill and Hillary Clinton invested in Whitewater Development Corporation. It was a land development project in Arkansas, and they partnered with Jim and Susan McDougal. It lost money and failed. Simple as that.

But when Bill Clinton became president, questions came up. Documents about Whitewater's finances were subpoenaed. People wanted to know if the Clintons had improperly benefited. And they wanted to know whether James McDougal, who ran a savings and loan, had received favorable regulatory treatment. It wasn't clear he had, but the questions needed answers.

In 1994, Attorney General Janet Reno appointed an independent counsel. First Robert B. Fiske Jr., then Kenneth Starr took over the investigation. Their job was simple: look into the land deal and related matters involving the Clintons and the McDougals.

The investigation lasted four years. It cost roughly seventy million dollars. And at the end of it all, no charges were brought against Bill or Hillary Clinton regarding Whitewater. James and Susan McDougal were convicted of fraud, but that was for other schemes, not Whitewater itself.

That's where the real problem started. Kenneth Starr's mandate kept expanding. His office began investigating White House personnel practices. Travel Gate. FBI File Gate. Then the investigation expanded even further to include the Lewinsky scandal. This scope creep fueled accusations of political bias. When Starr released his final report in 1998, he found insufficient evidence to prosecute the Clintons on Whitewater-related charges. But the investigation had consumed years and massive resources. It intensified public perception that the criminal justice system had been weaponized for political purposes. The scandal contributed to the broader polarization of the 1990s. Bill Clinton was the president whose investment and regulatory dealings were investigated. Hillary Clinton was the First Lady implicated in the financial matters. And Kenneth Starr was the independent counsel whose investigation eventually expanded far beyond its original mandate.
